questions.prompt: What does declaring a delegate field with the `event` keyword restrict?
options: It stops the publisher class itself from raising the event
It limits the event to a single handler
It makes the handlers run on a background thread
External code can mainly only subscribe (`+=`) and unsubscribe (`-=`)
questions.explanation: Events are encapsulated delegates; the `event` keyword restricts access so that external code is primarily allowed only to subscribe with `+=` and unsubscribe with `-=`.

questions.prompt: Put the stages of the publisher-subscriber model in order.
steps: The publisher declares an event using a delegate type
The subscriber registers its handler with the event using `+=`
The publisher's `On<EventName>` method invokes the event, calling all registered handlers
The subscriber detaches its handler with `-=` when it no longer needs notifications
questions.explanation: The publisher declares the event, subscribers attach handlers with `+=`, raising the event calls every registered handler, and subscribers can later detach with `-=`.

options: "Button is being clicked...", then "Button was clicked! (Handler executed)", then "Button is being clicked..."
"Button is being clicked...", then "Button was clicked! (Handler executed)", printed twice
"Button is being clicked..." twice, with no handler output
It throws a `NullReferenceException` on the second click, because the event has no subscribers
questions.explanation: The first click runs the handler. After `-=` removes it, `Click` has no subscribers, and `Click?.Invoke(...)` safely skips the call, so the second click prints only its own line.

questions.prompt: Why does `OnTemperatureChanged` copy the event into a local variable (`var handler = TemperatureChanged;`) before invoking it?
options: To make the event run faster
To avoid race conditions when the event is raised (thread-safety)
Because events can only be invoked through local variables
To stop subscribers from unsubscribing
questions.explanation: The best practices say to copy the delegate locally before invoking to avoid race conditions: `var h = Event; h?.Invoke(...)`.

questions.prompt: A short-lived UI control subscribes to an event on a long-lived service and never unsubscribes. What is the risk?
options: The service stops raising the event
The event handler runs twice
The control is leaked, because the publisher keeps a reference to it; unsubscribe in `Dispose` or use a weak-event pattern
Nothing; the garbage collector removes the handler automatically
questions.explanation: If the subscriber's lifetime is shorter than the publisher's, you must unsubscribe or use weak references, otherwise the subscriber leaks. The typical fix is unsubscribing in `Dispose`.

questions.prompt: An event has three handlers and the second one throws an exception. What happens?
options: Further handlers are stopped unless you handle the exception
The exception is ignored and all three handlers finish
The first handler is rolled back
The handlers are retried in reverse order
questions.explanation: Events are multicast; if one handler throws, it stops further handlers unless you handle exceptions, which is why libraries often iterate handlers manually.
